articles.title: Money in Bali: Cash, Cards and ATMs
articles.excerpt: Bali runs on rupiah, and you need both cards and cash. How to change money safely, what cards work, why US apps cannot pay by QR, and what gets added to every bill.
articles.content:
Bali runs on rupiah, and a visitor needs both a card and cash to get through a day comfortably. Plan on a card for the larger purchases and rupiah notes for the small ones. The rules around money are few, but each one costs a little if you ignore it, and this page sets them out in order.

The currency, and the rule about using it

The currency in Bali is the Indonesian rupiah, and prices are quoted in thousands and millions of it. Bali's 2025 rules for foreign visitors require transactions to be made in rupiah, so a price offered in US dollars is not how you should expect to pay. Carry rupiah for small purchases and a card for larger ones.

Getting used to the zeros

Rupiah amounts are large numbers: Bali's tourist levy, for example, is IDR 150,000 per person. Prices are sometimes written with the thousands dropped, as "150" or "150K". Count the zeros before you hand over notes; a 10,000 and a 100,000 note differ by one digit and a factor of ten.

Do not freeze an exchange rate in your head

The rupiah moves against the dollar, so check the rate when you travel instead of relying on a figure from an old article. Check the current rate on the day you travel and work out one easy rule of thumb for yourself, such as what 100,000 rupiah is worth in dollars this week.

Changing money without losing any

Bali's rules for visitors say to change money only at a licensed changer, and they describe how to recognize one. The 2025 circular tells foreign tourists to exchange currency only at authorized money changers, bank or non-bank, which are identified by a license number and a Bank Indonesia logo carrying a QR code.

What to look for

Look for the license number and the Bank Indonesia QR logo displayed at the counter before you hand anything over. A booth that cannot show them is not one the rules allow you to use, whatever rate it advertises on the board outside.

Our advice at the counter

This part is advice, not regulation. Agree the amount before the notes are counted, count the rupiah yourself in front of the cashier, and be the last person to touch the stack before it goes into your wallet. Do not let anyone recount it for you after you have checked it.

Cards and ATMs

Cards are the practical way to pay for the large items of a Bali trip, and a US card works for the official payments too. Indonesia's e-visa site takes Visa, Mastercard and JCB, and Bali's tourist levy site takes Visa, Mastercard, American Express and JCB. Bring at least two cards on different networks, kept in different bags.

Foreign transaction fees

Prices in Bali are charged in rupiah, so check before you leave whether your card adds a foreign transaction fee, and how much. Our advice is to carry a card that does not. When a terminal offers to charge you in dollars instead of rupiah, our advice is to choose rupiah and let your own bank do the conversion.

ATMs

We have not found an official source for withdrawal limits or operator fees at Bali's ATMs, and the figures in travel blogs disagree with each other, so we are not going to quote one. The part you can check before you go is your own bank's fee schedule for withdrawals abroad, and our advice is to read it.

Paying by QR code

QR payment is Indonesia's national standard, and Bali's rules for visitors tell tourists to use it, but the cross-border version is not open to American banking apps. Bank Indonesia's cross-border QR scheme connects Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea and China. The United States is not on that list.

For an American visitor that leaves cards and cash as the two working methods. The QR question has a page of its own, including what the central bank says and what it does not.

What gets added to the bill

Restaurant and hotel bills in Bali carry a local tax, and may also carry a separate service charge. In Badung regency, which covers Kuta, Seminyak, Canggu, Uluwatu and Nusa Dua, the local tax on restaurant food and drink and on hotel stays is 10%. Gianyar regency, which includes Ubud, sets the same rate.

Tax versus service charge

The two lines on a bill are different things. The tax goes to the local government. A service charge, under an Indonesian labor regulation covering hotels and hotel restaurants, is an amount added on top of the listed price for service, and it must be distributed to the staff. The regulation sets no percentage, so the rate is whatever the business has chosen.

Read the menu's small print

A menu or room rate may be quoted before tax and service. Our advice is to look for a line at the bottom of the menu saying whether prices include them, so the total does not surprise you.

Carrying cash across the border

Cash is not capped when you enter or leave Indonesia, but large amounts must be declared. Customs requires a declaration for money or other payment instruments worth IDR 100,000,000 or more, in rupiah or the foreign-currency equivalent. That is far more than a vacation calls for, so for most travelers the rule is one to know exists.

What this decision actually sits inside

Notice what happened across all of this. No single item was large: a foreign transaction fee, a conversion offered at the terminal, a tax line, a service line, a changer's rate. Each one is a small percentage, and they stack on the same dollar. The trip's real cost is the listed prices plus that stack, and the stack is decided by choices made at home: which cards you carry and what your bank charges.

How those small percentages add up across a whole trip, and which ones you can remove before you leave, is worked through in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Can I use US dollars in Bali?

Bali's rules for foreign visitors require transactions to be made in rupiah. Change dollars at a licensed money changer or withdraw rupiah from an ATM.

Can I use my credit card in Bali?

US cards work on the official visa and tourist levy sites, and a card is the practical way to pay for larger purchases. Carry rupiah cash for small ones.

How do I know a money changer in Bali is legitimate?

Authorized changers display a license number and a Bank Indonesia logo with a QR code. Bali's rules tell visitors to use only those.

Is tax included in restaurant prices in Bali?

Often not. In Badung and Gianyar regencies the local tax on restaurant food and drink is 10%, and many businesses add a separate service charge.

articles.title: Tipping in Bali: Service Charge, Tax and When to Add More
articles.excerpt: Tipping in Bali is optional, and many bills already include a service charge that goes to staff. How to read the tax and service lines, and when to leave more.
articles.content:
Tipping in Bali is optional, and the bill has often done part of the job already. Many hotel and restaurant bills include a service charge that, by regulation, goes to the staff, plus a local tax that does not. Once you can read those two lines, deciding what to leave on top becomes simple.

What is already on the bill

A restaurant or hotel bill in Bali can carry two additions to the menu price: a local tax and a service charge. In Badung regency, which covers Kuta, Seminyak, Canggu, Jimbaran, Uluwatu and Nusa Dua, the local tax on restaurant food and drink and on hotel stays is 10%.

The tax line

The tax is a regional government charge on food, drink and accommodation. Each regency sets its own rate; Gianyar regency, which includes Ubud, also sets it at 10% for restaurants and hotels. This money goes to the local government and has nothing to do with the people who served you.

The service line

A service charge is different. Under an Indonesian labor regulation, a service charge at a hotel or a hotel restaurant is an amount added on top of the listed price for service, and it must be distributed to the workers, half shared equally and the rest by seniority and performance, after allowances for breakage or loss and for staff development. The regulation sets no percentage, so the rate you see is the business's own.

Why this matters for tipping

If your bill shows a service charge at a hotel or hotel restaurant, part of what you paid is already going to the staff as a group. An extra tip is then a personal thank-you to the person who looked after you, not a correction to an unfair bill. Where no service charge appears, nothing has gone to the staff beyond their wages.

How to read "plus plus"

A price in Bali may be quoted before tax and service, with the two additions applied when the bill is totaled. A menu may mark this with a line of small print or with plus signs after the price. The total you pay is the listed price with both additions on top.

Check before you order

Our advice is to look at the foot of the menu for a line saying whether prices include tax and service. If it is not stated, ask. Where both are added, the total is higher than the menu price, and it is better to know that before you order.

The nightlife tax is much higher

One category is taxed differently. In Badung and Gianyar, entertainment at bars, nightclubs, discos, karaoke venues and spas was set at a 40% local tax by the regencies' 2023 tax regulations, in force from January 2024. That rate was publicly contested after it took effect and may have been amended since, so look at how a venue states its prices instead of assuming a figure.

When to leave more, and how

Tipping beyond the bill is a personal choice in Bali, with no official rule or fixed percentage behind it. We could not find an authoritative source for customary amounts, and the figures quoted on travel sites vary widely. The suggestions here are our own view of what is reasonable, not a local standard.

Restaurants and cafes

Where a service charge is on the bill, leaving nothing further is fine. Where it is not, rounding the bill up or leaving a modest amount in cash is a kind gesture that will be appreciated. Give it directly to your server if you want it to reach that person.

Drivers and guides

A driver who has spent the day with you, or a guide on a trek or tour, has given you a personal service that no bill line covers. A cash tip at the end of the day is appropriate if you were happy. Decide the amount by how long they worked and how much they added to your day.

Hotel staff and spa therapists

For housekeeping, porters and spa therapists, a small cash tip handed over personally is the clearest way to say thank you. If the hotel adds a service charge, the staff already share in it, and an individual tip is an extra.

Practical points about paying tips

Tips in Bali are best given in rupiah cash, handed to the person you mean to thank. Bali's rules for foreign visitors require transactions to be in rupiah, and small rupiah notes are useful all day for exactly this. Keep a separate fold of small notes so you are not searching for change.

Cash versus card

If you add a tip to a card payment, you have no way of knowing how it is distributed. Cash handed to an individual removes the question.

Do not tip in coins or foreign change

Our advice is to tip in rupiah. Foreign coins are the least useful thing to leave, because the person receiving them has to find a way to change them; if all you have is dollars, a banknote is better than coins.

Bargaining is separate from tipping

Bargaining and tipping are two different customs, and mixing them causes awkwardness. Our view is that a price you have agreed with a market stall or an independent driver is the whole price, and adding to it is your choice.

Agree the price first

For anything without a posted price, such as a day with a driver, agree the total and what it covers before you set off. Then a tip at the end is clearly a gift, and neither side is left guessing.

FAQ

Do you tip in Bali?

Tipping is optional. A hotel or restaurant bill may already include a service charge, which at hotels must by regulation be distributed to staff, and an extra cash tip is a personal thank-you.

Is service charge included in Bali restaurants?

Many businesses add one, on top of a local tax. The service charge rate is set by the business; the local tax on restaurant food and drink is 10% in Badung and Gianyar regencies.

Should I tip in rupiah or dollars?

Rupiah. Bali's rules for visitors require transactions in rupiah, and foreign coins cannot be exchanged.

How much is tax on a restaurant bill in Bali?

The local tax on restaurant food and drink is 10% in Badung and Gianyar regencies. Bars, nightclubs and spas are subject to a much higher entertainment tax.

articles.title: Paying by QR Code in Bali: Can Foreign Cards and Apps Use It?
articles.excerpt: QR codes are Indonesia's standard way to pay, but the cross-border scheme does not include the United States. What the central bank says and what Americans should carry.
articles.content:
QR codes are Indonesia's standard way to pay, and Bali's own rules tell visitors to use them. For Americans there is a catch: the cross-border system that lets foreigners scan those codes with their home banking app does not include the United States. Here is what the central bank says, and what to carry instead.

What the QR codes are

The QR codes at shops and restaurants in Bali belong to QRIS, Indonesia's national standard for QR payments, which is run under Bank Indonesia, the central bank. A customer scans the merchant's code with a payment app, enters the amount in rupiah and confirms. It is a single national standard, not one company's product.

Why visitors keep hearing about it

Bali's 2025 rules for foreign visitors tell tourists to make payments using Indonesia's standard QR code and to transact in rupiah. The province's tourist levy site also lists QRIS among its payment methods. So the system is part of the official picture a visitor is given, even if not every visitor can use it.

Which foreign visitors can scan and pay

Foreign visitors can pay by QRIS only if their home country is connected to Indonesia's cross-border scheme. Bank Indonesia lists the connected countries as Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea and China. A visitor from one of those opens a home payment app, scans, enters the rupiah amount and confirms in their own currency.

How the cross-border version works

Bank Indonesia describes the steps for a foreign user: open the payment application, scan the QRIS code, enter the payment amount in rupiah, confirm the destination and the amount in your own currency, and enter a PIN. The merchant uses the same printed code as for domestic customers. The conversion happens inside the visitor's own app.

Where the United States stands

The United States is not among the connected countries, and it does not appear anywhere on Bank Indonesia's page about the scheme. That means a US bank's app or a US digital wallet has no cross-border route to pay a QRIS code. Scanning the code with your phone's camera will not produce a payment screen you can use.

What an American should carry instead

An American visitor to Bali pays with cards and rupiah cash. Cards cover the official payments: Indonesia's e-visa site accepts Visa, Mastercard and JCB, and Bali's tourist levy site accepts Visa, Mastercard, American Express and JCB. Cash covers the small purchases where a QR code would have been the local customer's choice.

Cards

Bring two cards on different networks and keep them apart. If your card charges a foreign transaction fee, it applies to every purchase in Bali, so a card without one is worth carrying. When a terminal offers to bill you in dollars, our advice is to choose rupiah.

Cash

Keep a supply of small rupiah notes. Change money only at authorized changers, which Bali's rules identify by a license number and a Bank Indonesia logo with a QR code, or withdraw rupiah from an ATM.

Official fees

The payments a visitor owes the authorities do not depend on QR. The visa fee and the tourist levy can both be paid by card on their official sites before you leave home, which is the simplest way to deal with them. The levy site lists QRIS as one option among several, and a card works in its place.

If a place takes only QR

Ask whether cash is accepted. Bali's rules require transactions in rupiah, and rupiah notes are legal tender. If a counter really cannot take cash or a card, you will need to buy elsewhere.

What about tourist wallets and local apps?

Whether a short-stay American can set up a local wallet to pay by QR is a question we could not settle from an official source. Bank Indonesia's page on the cross-border scheme describes payments from the connected countries and says nothing about a route for other visitors. Press reports describe products aimed at tourists, and we have not verified how they work for a US traveler.

Why we are not recommending a workaround

Without a source we trust on how a visitor would open and fund a local wallet, the honest advice is not to build a trip around QR payment. Plan on cards and cash.

If the list changes

Bank Indonesia has added countries to the scheme over time, and its page is the place to check. If the United States is added, American banking apps that take part would be able to pay a QRIS code the way visitors from the connected countries do now.

Reading a QR code is not paying it

Paying with a QRIS code needs a payment app that is connected to the scheme; a phone's camera can read the code, but that alone does not move any money. Pointing a phone camera at it, or using a generic QR reader, shows a string of characters or an error. If a seller asks you to scan a code and you are an American visitor, the practical answer is to ask for the card terminal or pay in cash.

Be careful with payment links

Our advice applies anywhere: do not enter card details into a web page that a QR code opened unless you can see it is the business's own or a payment provider you recognize. The official sites for Indonesia's visa and Bali's tourist levy are reached by typing their addresses, not by scanning a code on a poster.

FAQ

Can Americans use QRIS in Bali?

Not through US banking apps. Bank Indonesia's cross-border QR scheme connects Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea and China; the United States is not included.

Does Apple Pay work with QR codes in Bali?

QRIS codes are paid through apps that belong to Indonesia's QR scheme. Bank Indonesia's list of connected countries does not include the United States.

How should Americans pay in Bali?

With cards for larger purchases and rupiah cash for small ones. The official visa and tourist levy sites accept major US card networks.

What is QRIS?

QRIS is Indonesia's national QR payment standard, run under Bank Indonesia. It is a single standard used across the country.

articles.title: Indonesia's Phone Registration Rule: Do Tourists Need It?
articles.excerpt: Indonesia blocks unregistered phones from its networks, but customs says short-stay tourists do not need to register. Here are the two cases that keep you clear.
articles.content:
No. A tourist visiting Bali for a normal vacation does not need to register a phone with Indonesian customs. Indonesia does have a phone registration system that ties lasting use of its mobile networks to a registered device, but customs itself says short-stay visitors are outside it in the two ways that matter. The confusion comes from rules written for residents.

What the registration system is

Indonesia runs an IMEI registration system for phones brought in from abroad, and its customs service publishes the rules. The IMEI is the identifying number of a phone. Customs sets out two cases in which a short-stay visitor does not need to register at all.

Why it exists

The system is about imported devices and the duty owed on them. Indonesian customs lists IMEI registration among the matters a passenger declares on arrival, alongside goods above the duty-free value. A resident bringing a new phone home from abroad is the case it was built for.

What customs says about tourists

Indonesian customs answers the tourist question directly in its own guidance. For a person staying only temporarily, such as a tourist or business visitor, IMEI registration is not required in two situations: when the phone keeps using its home SIM on roaming, and when the visitor uses an Indonesian SIM registered at a mobile operator's outlet.

If you roam on your US plan

A phone that keeps its American SIM and connects through your US carrier's roaming is not affected. The registration rule concerns devices using an Indonesian signal provider, and a roaming phone is still a customer of its home network. Check your carrier's international rates before you rely on this for a whole trip.

If you buy a local SIM

A visitor who wants a local number registers the SIM at an operator's outlet, and customs says this gives network access for up to 90 days. That covers any trip on a 30-day tourist visa, including one that is extended. Our advice is to bring your passport to the outlet.

Where a travel eSIM fits

A travel eSIM bought from an international provider before you leave works like roaming from the phone's point of view: the plan belongs to a foreign provider and connects through partner networks in Indonesia. Customs' guidance names roaming on a home SIM and a local SIM registered at an outlet; it does not mention travel eSIMs by name.

Our reading

We read a foreign travel eSIM as falling on the roaming side of that line, since it is not an Indonesian subscription. That is an inference from the wording, not a statement by customs. If you want certainty, the two cases customs does name are the safe ones: your own carrier's roaming, or a local SIM set up at an operator's shop.

Check that your phone is unlocked

A local SIM or a travel eSIM only works in a phone that is not locked to your US carrier. This is a matter between you and your carrier, separate from Indonesian rules. Ask your carrier before you travel.

What to do at the airport

An American tourist on a short stay does not need to visit the customs registration desk for a personal phone. If you plan to roam or to use a local SIM from an operator's outlet, customs' own guidance says registration is not required, so you can walk past the counter with a clear conscience.

When the answer is different

The picture changes for someone staying long term. The 90-day access that comes with an outlet-registered tourist SIM is a limit as well as an allowance. Anyone planning to stay beyond that, or to leave a phone behind in Indonesia, is in the situation the registration system was designed for and should read the customs rules for residents.

Bringing a new, boxed phone

A brand-new phone in a sealed box is a different matter from the one in your pocket. Customs allows personal goods up to USD 500 per person free of duty and treats goods that are not for personal use as a declaration matter. A device you are bringing as a gift for someone who lives in Indonesia is outside the two visitor cases above, so ask customs at arrival how it should be handled.

Choosing how to stay connected

The registration rule leaves an American tourist three workable options for mobile service in Bali: roaming on a US plan, a travel eSIM bought in advance, or a local SIM bought at an operator's outlet. None of them requires dealing with customs. The choice comes down to cost, convenience and whether you want a local number.

Roaming

Roaming is the least effort, and the cost depends entirely on your US plan, so check its international rates. It keeps your US number working for calls and verification texts, which matters for banking apps that send codes by text.

Travel eSIM

A travel eSIM is set up before you fly and connects when you land, with no shop visit. Many such plans provide data only, in which case your US number remains on your physical SIM for texts if you leave that line switched on.

Local SIM

A local SIM gives you an Indonesian number, which is useful for apps and services that expect one. Buy it at an operator's own outlet, since that is the route customs names, and expect to show your passport.

FAQ

Do tourists need to register their phone in Bali?

No. Indonesian customs says IMEI registration is not required for short-stay visitors who roam on their home SIM or who use an Indonesian SIM registered at a mobile operator's outlet.

Will my phone be blocked in Indonesia?

Not on a normal vacation. A tourist SIM registered at an operator's outlet gives network access for up to 90 days, and a phone roaming on its home SIM is not affected.

Do I have to pay tax on my phone when entering Bali?

A personal phone you are carrying for your own use on a short visit does not need registration. A new, boxed device brought as a gift is an import and is treated differently.

Does a travel eSIM need IMEI registration in Indonesia?

Customs' guidance does not mention travel eSIMs by name. It exempts short-stay visitors roaming on a home SIM; we read a foreign travel eSIM as falling on that side, which is our inference.

articles.title: Visa on Arrival vs. e-VOA for Bali: Which to Get
articles.excerpt: The visa on arrival and the e-VOA are the same Indonesian tourist visa at the same price. The difference is where you do the paperwork. Here is how to choose.
articles.content:
They are the same visa. The visa on arrival and the e-VOA both give an American the same B1 tourist visa, at the same official price, for the same 30 days. The only real difference is where you do the paperwork: at your kitchen table before you fly, or at a counter in the airport after a very long journey.

What you get either way

The visa on arrival and the e-VOA are two ways of buying Indonesia's B1 tourist visa, and the result is identical. Either route costs IDR 500,000 and gives a stay of 30 days, extendable once for another 30 days. The same rules about what you may do in Indonesia apply to both.

What the letters mean

VOA stands for visa on arrival. The "e" in e-VOA means electronic: the same visa, applied and paid for online in advance. Indonesia's official e-visa site lists it for US passport holders as "B1 - Tourist (Visa On Arrival)". If you see the two terms treated as different products with different prices, you are probably looking at an agency's page.

The case for buying online first

Buying the e-VOA before you fly moves the payment and form-filling out of the airport, and the State Department notes that travelers who wait to buy at the airport may face long lines. There is no nonstop flight from the United States to Bali, so the visa counter comes at the end of a long journey with at least one connection.

How the online route works

You apply on Indonesia's official e-visa website, run by the Directorate General of Immigration, and pay by Visa, Mastercard or JCB card. One application can cover up to five people, which suits a family. The application asks for your departure date and a booked return flight. Once approved, the visa is sent as a download link by email.

How early to do it

The visa is valid for entry for 90 days, so it can be bought well ahead. Our advice is to do it once your flights are booked and your passport details are final, leaving time to sort out any problem with the application before you travel.

What can go wrong online

The main risk online is the wrong website. Third-party sites may charge a fee on top of the official price for the same application. Use the address printed on the State Department's Indonesia page, and check that the price you are asked for matches the official one.

The case for buying at the airport

Buying the visa on arrival at the airport needs no preparation, which makes it the fallback for a trip booked at short notice or an application left too late. The State Department confirms that a traveler can purchase a visa upon arrival at the airport, at a booth located before the immigration counters.

What it costs you

The price is the same. The cost is time and attention at the end of a long travel day: a payment counter first, then the immigration line.

When it is the right choice

The airport route makes sense if you could not complete the online application, if your plans changed at the last moment, or if you are uneasy about entering card details on a website you are not sure is the official one. It is a perfectly valid way to enter Bali.

What neither route changes

Choosing the e-VOA or the airport counter does not change the entry requirements that actually turn people away. A US passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond your arrival date and have 2 blank pages, and immigration can ask to see an outbound ticket from Indonesia.

The arrival card is separate

Every traveler also completes Indonesia's arrival card, which is free and separate from the visa. It only opens shortly before travel: fill it in during the last two days before you land, and save the QR code it produces.

So is the tourist levy

Bali's tourist levy is a third item, charged by the province, at IDR 150,000 per person. Paying for an e-VOA does not pay the levy.

Extending either one

Both versions of the visa can be extended once, for another 30 days, and the official fee for a 30-day stay permit is IDR 500,000 per application. Indonesia's e-visa site has an "Extend My Visa" function for visas issued through it.

If you think you might stay longer

We could not confirm from an official source whether a visa bought at the airport counter can be extended through the website in the same way. If there is a real chance you will stay past 30 days, buying the e-VOA online is the more cautious choice, since the online extension function belongs to the same system.

Start the extension early

Whichever route you used, begin the extension well before the first 30 days end. An expired visa is an overstay, and overstaying carries a fine of IDR 1,000,000 per day.

Our recommendation

For most Americans the e-VOA is the better choice, because it removes a line from the worst moment of the journey and costs the same. Buy it on the official site after your flights are booked. If that does not work out, the airport counter is there. Where the visa sits among the other pre-flight steps is laid out in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Is the e-VOA the same as the visa on arrival?

Yes. Both are Indonesia's B1 tourist visa, with the same official fee and the same 30-day stay. The e-VOA is bought online in advance; the visa on arrival is bought at the airport.

Is the e-VOA cheaper than the visa on arrival?

No. The official fee is the same either way. A higher price online usually means a third-party agency.

How long before my trip can I get an e-VOA?

The visa is valid for entry for 90 days, so it can be bought well in advance.

Can I still get a visa at Bali airport?

Yes. The State Department confirms a visa can be purchased on arrival at the airport, at a booth before the immigration counters.
